blogs.title: The 'Stale' Declaration Problem: How D.C. Circuit Preserves Exemption 7(A) Validity Across Years
blogs.description: This post analyzes the procedural tension in *Farahi* regarding the passage of time between the initial FOIA litigation and final resolution. While the D.C. Circuit has previously warned that vague assertions of ongoing investigations may become insufficient over time (*CREW*), Judge Katsas clarifies that a subsequent, albeit terse, declarant (Bender) can validate earlier, detailed findings (Hardy) rather than starting from scratch. The analysis explores how courts should manage multi-year FOIA disputes involving sensitive national security matters and whether this approach strengthens or weakens judicial oversight of agency delay tactics.

blogs.title: The Invisibility of Justice: The Expanding Role of Ex Parte Declarations in National Security FOIA Litigation
blogs.description: Focusing on the structural implications of the ruling, this article examines the court's robust defense of relying on ex parte and in camera submissions to resolve segregability and exemption claims. By affirming that plaintiffs forfeit challenges to ex parte reliance if they do not initially object, and by noting that such secrecy is 'inherent' to national security cases, the opinion signals a continued deference to executive confidentiality. The post discusses how this dynamic creates an asymmetry in adversarial testing and what it means for transparency advocates challenging terrorism-related files.

blogs.title: 'Interspersed Line-by-Line': Reaffirming the High Bar for Segregability in Counterterrorism Files
blogs.description: This post dissects the court's application of FOIA's segregability requirement (§ 552(b)) in the context of complex counterterrorism dossiers. Addressing Farahi's argument that 'some' non-exempt words must be released from thousands of pages, Judge Katsas reiterates the *Mead Data Central* standard: if non-exempt material is randomly interspersed throughout a document such that releasing it would compromise the exempt core, no segregation is required. The analysis considers how this doctrine effectively allows agencies to withhold entire files containing minor redactable elements when those elements are woven into a tapestry of national security intelligence.
